title: Value at Risk: three ways to compute it, and what it misses

creativeDirection: Editorial quant notebook at night. Near-black canvas with a faint warm wash and film grain; one heavy, tightly tracked headline per slide; justified bold body copy in a single column; gold labels name the method; real LaTeX equations float in the corners as quiet texture and one hero equation carries the maths. illustration.purpose: Sets the theme: a portfolio's future is a fan of random paths; VaR summarises its bad tail.

slides.headline: WHAT VaR SAYS
slides.label: One number, one confidence level, one horizon
body: VaR answers a single question: over the next day, what loss will we not exceed with 99% confidence? It is a quantile of the P&L distribution, nothing more.
A 1-day 99% VaR of $279k means losses should exceed $279k on about 1 day in 100. It says nothing about how large those bad days get.

illustration.purpose: Shows VaR as the cut-off point of the left tail of the P&L distribution.

slides.headline: 1. PARAMETRIC
slides.label: Variance–covariance method
body: Assume returns are normal. VaR is then volatility scaled by a z-score: portfolio σ comes from the covariance matrix and your position weights.
$10M portfolio, 1.2% daily σ: 2.326 × 1.2% × $10M ≈ $279k. Fast and analytic, but it inherits the normal distribution's thin tails.

illustration.purpose: The covariance matrix assembling cell by cell: the single input the parametric method needs beyond weights.

slides.headline: 2. HISTORICAL
slides.label: Historical simulation
body: No distribution assumed. Replay the last 500 days of market moves on today's portfolio, sort the P&Ls, and read off the loss at the cut-off.
At 99% with 500 scenarios, VaR is about the 5th-worst loss. Real fat tails are captured, but only the ones in your window: a calm 500 days gives a calm VaR.

illustration.purpose: 500 historical P&Ls sorted from worst to best, with the five worst highlighted and the VaR cut-off drawn.

slides.headline: 3. MONTE CARLO
slides.label: Simulate the future instead of replaying the past
body: Choose a model for every risk factor, simulate thousands of scenarios, reprice the portfolio in each, and take the loss quantile of the simulated P&L.
It handles options and other non-linear payoffs that the parametric method misses. The price: compute time, and answers only as good as the model.

illustration.purpose: Simulated price paths fan out from today's price; the terminal histogram and its low quantile give the VaR.

slides.headline: SCALE & BACKTEST
slides.label: √time scaling and the Basel traffic light
body: Regulators asked for 10-day VaR, usually scaled from 1-day: $279k × √10 ≈ $883k. That holds only if daily returns are independent and identically distributed.
Then test the model: over 250 days a 99% VaR should be breached about 2.5 times. Basel counts the exceptions: 0–4 green, 5–9 yellow, 10 or more red.

illustration.purpose: A year of daily P&L against the 99% VaR line; three breaches circled, landing in the green zone.

slides.headline: WHAT VaR MISSES
body: VaR marks where the tail starts, not how deep it goes. Two portfolios can share a VaR while one hides a far worse tail.
Expected Shortfall averages the losses beyond VaR. Basel's FRTB swapped 99% VaR for 97.5% ES: equal-ish under normality (2.338σ vs 2.326σ), but ES grows when tails get fat.

illustration.purpose: Same distribution, with Expected Shortfall marked deeper in the tail than VaR.

slides.footnote: Figures assume normally distributed daily P&L; real P&L has fatter tails.
